issue: No declared mandatory-field metadata exists on the API surface under test. Of 5,175 body properties across 1,306 endpoints, 0 carry a machine-readable required declaration. The 3 [Required] attributes that exist in pam/PAM bind to no tested endpoint.
recommended_solution: Annotate request models with [Required] in the gateway microservices and enable model-state validation in the request pipeline, starting with the 217 create endpoints (1,245 body properties). Roll out per controller.
recommended_advantages: Turns metadata into enforced behaviour rather than documentation. One class of change simultaneously fixes server-side validation, enables generated documentation and unblocks test generation. Incremental and shippable controller by controller, so value lands before the whole surface is done.
recommended_disadvantages: Touches many separate microservices. Enabling model-state validation can begin rejecting payloads that existing clients send successfully today, so it needs a compatibility pass and probably a feature flag per service. The work is invisible to end users, so it competes poorly for prioritisation.
alternative_solution: Generate and publish an OpenAPI document from the live gateway microservices with required[] populated, and treat it as the contract of record.
alternative_advantages: No product code change. Machine-readable for every consumer, not just this test suite. Can cover endpoints whose source was never supplied to QA, which is 96.3% of the surface.
alternative_disadvantages: Documentation only — nothing is enforced server-side, so the document can drift from actual behaviour and there is no mechanism that detects the drift. Repeats the existing failure mode where the Confluence export is known to be out of date.

issue: No length, format, pattern or range metadata exists anywhere on the surface. Twelve DataAnnotations families ([StringLength], [MaxLength], [MinLength], [Range], [RegularExpression], [EmailAddress], [Phone], [Url], [Compare], [DataType], [AllowedValues], Newtonsoft Required=Always) return 0 occurrences across 6,866 .cs files.
recommended_solution: Add [StringLength], [Range] and [RegularExpression] to request models, deriving the values from the existing database column definitions, which already encode length, type and nullability.
recommended_advantages: The constraints already exist in the schema — this publishes them rather than inventing them, so the values are defensible. Unlocks boundary and format negative testing across 5,175 properties at once. Also improves error quality, because a declarative rule can be cited in the message.
recommended_disadvantages: A database column length is not always the intended API contract, so some values need a product decision rather than a lookup. Mapping column to property is manual wherever the names differ, and naming is known to be inconsistent (see A5-07).
alternative_solution: Publish a data-dictionary export (table, column, data type, length, nullability) and have the test harness derive boundary values from it, without changing product code.
alternative_advantages: Very cheap and fast — largely a schema query. Requires no product-code change and no release. Immediately unlocks boundary-test generation for the properties that can be mapped to a column.
alternative_disadvantages: Not enforced anywhere, so the API can still accept input the database will reject — which is the current defect restated rather than fixed. Only covers properties that map cleanly to a column; computed and pass-through fields get nothing.
owner_team: PAM API Development (gateway microservice owners), with DBA support for the column export

issue: Mandatory-ness is discoverable only by sending a bad request and parsing prose. The same fact is expressed in five different message grammars across 41 distinct rejection messages, and the rule text is not stable ('PageSize is required should be greater than 0.' and 'PageSize is required and should be greater than 0.' occurred in the same run).
recommended_solution: Return a structured field-level error object — {errors:[{field, rule, message}]} — replacing all five prose grammars with one machine-readable shape.
recommended_advantages: Removes prose parsing entirely and makes negative assertions exact rather than substring matches. Resolves LH-04 in the same change. A consumer learns the field and the rule that failed, not a sentence it has to interpret.
recommended_disadvantages: A response-shape change: any existing client parsing message text breaks, so it needs versioning or a feature flag. Does not by itself tell a consumer the rules in advance — it still requires a failed call to learn them.
alternative_solution: Expose a describe endpoint per operation returning its required fields, types and bounds. GET /api/Service/ServiceMandatoryFields already exists in the surface as a working precedent.
alternative_advantages: Rules are discoverable without sending a bad request, which matters here because a probing call on this API may be a mutating call that safety rules forbid replaying. No change to the validation path or to existing response shapes. The pattern already ships, so it needs no architectural argument.
alternative_disadvantages: Creates a second source of truth that can drift from the code that actually enforces validation, unless it is generated from the same models. Needs to be built for every operation to be useful, and partial coverage misleads.
evidence_ref: artifacts/analysis-data/required-fields-summary.json (observed_mandatory_set.prose_grammar_counts: json-deserialiser=123, procedural=64, is-required=30, model-state=8, null-check=3; distinct_rejection_messages=41); docs/analysis/A5-mandatory-field-analysis.md §4; artifacts/runs/2026-07-29_181439/results.json

issue: 185 of 217 create endpoints (85.3%) have no mandatory-field signal of any kind, and 66 have no known properties at all. Only 32 of 217 (14.7%) have any mandatory-field metadata, and 29 of those signals were recovered from rejection messages rather than read from a contract. Measured consequence: 13 of 217 creates insert successfully.
recommended_solution: Ask the developers for one known-good request body per create endpoint, captured from their own integration tests or Postman collections.
recommended_advantages: The cheapest route to the largest coverage gain available — developer time is minutes per endpoint. A single real payload simultaneously settles which fields are mandatory, what types they take and what values are valid. Precedent exists: when two payloads were corrected by hand after reading the error text, both inserted successfully the same day on the same environment, which is why this is a metadata problem and not a tooling problem.
recommended_disadvantages: Depends entirely on another team's schedule and goodwill. A captured fixture is a sample, not a contract, so it goes stale silently as the API evolves. Does not generalise — it fixes the endpoints supplied and nothing else.
alternative_solution: Build a curated fixture library inside the harness from the 224 observed-mandatory properties plus the 1,654 endpoint-bound documented payloads, and grow it by differential probing within the safety rules.
alternative_advantages: Requires nothing from any other team, so it can start immediately. Builds on evidence already retained rather than new access. Compounds — each create that starts working yields observed chain keys that unlock further hops.
alternative_disadvantages: Slow, and encodes current behaviour including its defects. Probing means sending mutating calls, which the safety rules restrict and which cannot be replayed. Confluence payloads bind to endpoints by page proximity, so some fixtures will be built on a wrong binding.
owner_team: PAM API Development (payload capture) with QA Automation (fixture library)
evidence_ref: artifacts/analysis-data/required-fields-summary.json (create_endpoints: total=217, with_ANY_mandatory_field_metadata=32, no_mandatory_signal_at_all=185, zero_properties_known=66, measured_outcome.re_derived_strict=13); docs/analysis/A5-mandatory-field-analysis.md §5.1; artifacts/loopholes/LH-10 EVIDENCE.md §3

issue: Negative testing is structurally unassertable. The ExpectedErrorCode column is absent from all 151 header blocks of the negative data workbook, so 0 of 3,167 rows assert an error code. 3,154 rows (99.6%) target HTTP 405 or 401 and never reach application code; the 13 rows that do target application validation assert only ExpectedStatus=200, which passes whether the request was correctly rejected or wrongly accepted. Across the derived property-level scenario space, 20,469 of 20,700 scenarios (98.9%) cannot be authored truthfully.
recommended_solution: Publish the application error-code register and add an ExpectedErrorCode column to the negative data schema. The framework parameter validateApiResponseWithResponseTime_ExcelBasedsettingnegative(...) is already plumbed for it — only the register and the data column are missing.
recommended_advantages: Converts the 13 currently unassertable application rows into real assertions and unblocks thousands more. It is the only option that can catch 'this should have been rejected and was not', which a baseline cannot. Most of the framework work is already done, so the cost is data and documentation rather than code.
recommended_disadvantages: Depends on a register that does not exist — 4 error codes are documented against 108 observed live, and the framework's KNOWN_ERROR_CODES set {201,202,203} is already known to be incomplete (a live run captured 206-LC_GLD). Until the register lands, the column has nothing authoritative to hold.
alternative_solution: Freeze a differential baseline: observe each rejection once, record status plus errorCode plus message, and assert future runs against the frozen value.
alternative_advantages: Available immediately with no product dependency and no other team involved. Detects any future change in rejection behaviour, including unintended ones. A legitimate technique and the right interim move while the register is produced.
alternative_disadvantages: Locks in current behaviour as correct, defects included. Structurally cannot detect input that should be rejected and never was, which is the most valuable class of negative test. Requires sending each bad request once, which for mutating endpoints the safety rules restrict.
owner_team: PAM API Development (error-code register) with QA Automation (data schema and baseline)

issue: The published metric materially understates the gap. '3 [Required] of 6,738 properties' uses the whole .NET product as its denominator, but pam/PAM implements only 48 of 1,306 catalogue endpoints (3.7%). All three [Required] attributes sit on one ProvisioningService data-access class whose property names appear in none of the 5,940 mapped endpoint properties, and no Provisioning* controller exists among the 70. On the surface actually under test the count is 0 of 5,175.
recommended_solution: Re-scope the metric to the surface under test and publish '0 of 5,175' alongside '3 of 6,738', stating explicitly that the three declarations bind to no tested endpoint.
recommended_advantages: Costs almost nothing and corrects a figure that changes how the finding reads: '3' invites 'so it is nearly there', whereas '0' is unambiguous. Removes an objection a developer would reasonably raise on seeing the original ratio. Keeps both numbers so neither prior report is contradicted.
recommended_disadvantages: A reporting change only — it fixes no behaviour and closes no gap. Two numbers for one fact must be explained every time they are quoted, which adds friction to the write-up.
alternative_solution: Obtain the gateway microservice sources so that static analysis runs against the request models actually serving the API, making the denominator meaningful.
alternative_advantages: Makes every static metric meaningful rather than merely honest about its own irrelevance. Would let this entire analysis run against the real request models, which is the only way to measure the true declared-metadata coverage. Also unblocks A5-01 estimation, which is currently guesswork.
alternative_disadvantages: An access and coordination dependency outside QA's control. 96.3% of the surface is currently outside the snapshot, so the ask is large. Does not itself improve the product.
owner_team: QA Automation (reporting) with PAM API Development (source access)

issue: Field names are not canonical, so even the recovered mandatory set is unreliable for generation. The 37 property names the server named in rejections include UserId, UserID and UsrId; LOBId and LOBID; ServiceId, ServiceID and Service_ID; ServiceUserName and Service_Username. A consumer cannot tell a spelling variant from a genuinely different field.
recommended_solution: Publish a canonical field-name registry and accept the historical spellings as explicit serializer aliases on the request models.
recommended_advantages: Fixes the ambiguity for every consumer rather than only for this test suite. Makes generated clients, documentation and validators coherent. Aliases preserve backward compatibility, so no existing caller breaks.
recommended_disadvantages: Touches many services. Aliases must be maintained indefinitely for compatibility, so the inconsistency is documented forever rather than removed. Deciding the canonical form requires a product owner, not just a developer.
alternative_solution: Normalise case and separators in the harness only, treating UserId, UserID and UsrId as one logical field for chaining and generation.
alternative_advantages: Cheap and entirely within QA's control, and partly implemented already via case-insensitive chain matching. Immediately improves chain-key resolution without waiting on anyone.
alternative_disadvantages: Does not fix the API — a real consumer still faces the ambiguity. Risks silently merging two genuinely different fields that differ only in case or separator, which would produce wrong payloads that are hard to diagnose. Masks the defect rather than reporting it.
owner_team: PAM API Development (registry) with QA Automation (harness normalisation)

issue: docs/briefs/developer-loopholes.md §10 — the stated source of truth for the 12 findings — disagrees with its own generated evidence pack on three sub-figures: public classes 5,262 vs 5,994, [Range] 5 vs 0, [JsonProperty] 7 vs 11. An independent re-scan confirms the generated pack (5,994 / 0 / 11). The [Range]=5 error understates the finding, since [Range] does not occur at all.
recommended_solution: Correct §10 from the generated pack — public classes 5,262 to 5,994, [Range] 5 to 0, [JsonProperty] 7 to 11 — and cite tools/lh_specs_static.py as the generator so the figures are traceable.
recommended_advantages: The stated source of truth stops contradicting its own evidence. Corrects a figure that understates the finding, since 'five [Range] attributes exist' invites the reply that some validation is present when none is. Citing the generator prevents the same drift recurring.
recommended_disadvantages: The file is hand-written and will drift again unless the figures are regenerated rather than retyped. Touching a source-of-truth document invites re-review of the surrounding text.
alternative_solution: Mark the three sub-figures as superseded in place and cite artifacts/loopholes/LH-10-no-validation-attributes-on-models/EVIDENCE.md as authoritative for the attribute census.
alternative_advantages: Preserves the document as written, which suits an append-only convention, while removing the risk that someone quotes a wrong figure. Faster than reconciling the prose.
alternative_disadvantages: Leaves two numbers in circulation for the same fact, so a reader must know which to trust. Adds clutter to a document whose value is being the single clear statement of each finding.

issue: Acknowledged creates return no identifier. Of the 196 L5 'MISSING [NEW_ID]' chain failures, 19 followed a create the server accepted whose response carried no id for the created record. This is independent of the mandatory-field gap — no amount of request metadata fixes it. Root-cause split of the 196: 117 create genuinely failed, 19 acknowledged but no identifier returned, 0 extractor bugs, 60 indeterminate.
recommended_solution: Return the created record's identifier in the create response — {Success, Message, Result:{Id}} — across all 217 create endpoints.
recommended_advantages: This is the standard create contract and the single change that unblocks chaining, read-back and teardown for every consumer rather than just for tests. Removes a whole class of guesswork: a client currently cannot learn what it just created, so it cannot verify, update or delete it. Also makes persistence verifiable, which is currently proven for only 2 writes in 1,868 calls.
recommended_disadvantages: A response-shape change across 217 endpoints, so it needs versioning or a feature flag for existing clients. Some creates are bulk or fire-and-forget and have no single natural identifier, so those need a per-endpoint decision.
alternative_solution: Have the harness resolve the identifier with a follow-up read, matching on the values just submitted.
alternative_advantages: Requires no product change and works against endpoints exactly as they ship today. Can be implemented selectively for the highest-value chains first.
alternative_disadvantages: Fragile, and sometimes impossible: LOB names are AES-encrypted at rest (sso_lobs.sls_name holds base64 ciphertext), so matching a created record by the plaintext name submitted cannot work. Adds a read per create, needs a unique field to match on which is itself undeclared, and races against concurrent activity on a shared environment.
